sentences.text: This armored dinosaur is closely related to the genus Polacanthus.
Charles W. Gilmore estimated the animal stood roughly 4 feet tall at the hips and measured about 5 meters in total length.
The genus remains obscure because its remains were damaged, leading to past misinterpretations.
Its heavy armor served as the primary defense while it fed on low vegetation.
Nelson Horatio Darton found the holotype specimen USNM 4752 near Buffalo Gap Station in 1898.
Frederic Augustus Lucas initially named it a new species of Stegosaurus in 1901 before creating its own genus.
Charles W. Gilmore provided a full description of the material in 1914.
This quadrupedal herbivore likely grazed close to the ground.
Unlike Polacanthus, this species lacked a distinct tail club, possessing only prominent dorsal spines and tips.
The animal belongs to the family Nodosauridae.
It is placed within the subfamily Polacanthinae.
Modern classification treats it as either a polacanthine or polacanthid ankylosaur based on preference.
It inhabited the Lakota Formation of Custer County, South Dakota, during the Barremian stage.
This occurred approximately 130 million years ago in what is now North America.
Its time range extended from the Barremian to the Aptian stages, spanning between 125.77 and 113.2 million years ago.
William T. Blows and Javier Pereda-Suberbiola once argued Hoplitosaurus was synonymous with Polacanthus, but this view was later rejected.
Ken Carpenter and James Kirkland suggested that similarities between the two genera were either widespread among ankylosaurs or resulted from bone damage.
